stem: Shots rise from 1000 to 4000. How does the sampling error of an estimated outcome probability change?

options.text: It drops to a quarter, because the sampling error scales like 1/N with the shot count
It roughly halves — shot error scales like 1/sqrt(N)
It barely moves — statistical error is set by the device's noise level, not by the shot count
It roughly doubles, because a longer job accumulates more drift and readout error
It drops to roughly a sixteenth, since the variance falls like the square of the shot count
It typically stays put — the PUB count sets it

explanation.correct: Counting outcomes is a Monte-Carlo estimate of a probability. The standard error of a frequency is sqrt(p(1-p)/N), i.e. it shrinks like 1/sqrt(N). Quadrupling the shots (1000 -> 4000) multiplies the error by 1/sqrt(4) = 1/2. This is why halving the error costs 4x the shots — the same shots<->precision trade-off that underlies the primitives.

distractors.A: Sampling error scales like 1/sqrt(N), not 1/N. You would need 16x the shots (not 4x) to quarter the error.
distractors.C: Shot noise is a property of finite sampling and clearly decreases with more shots; it is not fixed by the hardware.
distractors.D: More shots reduce, not increase, the statistical uncertainty of the estimate; the error goes down like 1/sqrt(N).
distractors.E: The variance of a binomial proportion falls like 1/N, so the standard error falls like 1/sqrt(N): 4x more shots is 2x less error, not 16x.
distractors.F: The number of PUBs only says how many separate results come back; the sampling error of each estimate is governed by that PUB's shots.
